nameStory: Poison sumac gets its name from its toxic properties combined with its resemblance to the harmless sumacs in the cashew family. The word 'sumac' comes from Arabic 'summāq,' referring to the red, berry-like fruits that many sumacs produce. Despite sharing a family and common name, poison sumac is actually more closely related to poison ivy than to the friendly sumacs you might use for landscaping.
description: Poison sumac is a tall woody shrub or small tree that can reach up to 30 feet high, making it much larger than its notorious cousins poison ivy and poison oak. It has smooth, grayish bark and distinctive compound leaves with 7-13 leaflets arranged in pairs along a red stem. Unlike other sumacs, it produces drooping clusters of whitish berries and thrives in wet, swampy areas. Every part of this plant contains urushiol, the same oil that makes poison ivy so irritating to human skin.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-13 smooth-edged leaflets arranged in pairs along a reddish stem, with one leaflet at the tip. Leaflets are oval-shaped and feel smooth to the touch, lacking the teeth or serrations of harmless sumacs.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a tall shrub or small tree up to 30 feet high with an open, somewhat sparse branching pattern. Stems are smooth and often have a reddish tint.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Produces drooping clusters of small, whitish or pale yellow berries that hang down like grapes. These clusters feel papery when dry and persist into winter.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, thin bark that's gray to light brown in color. Unlike the deeply furrowed bark of many trees, poison sumac's bark remains relatively smooth even as it matures.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found in wet, swampy areas, bogs, and wetland edges where your feet might get soggy. This wetland preference immediately distinguishes it from upland sumacs.

habitat: Poison sumac is almost exclusively found in wetlands, swamps, bogs, and marshy areas throughout New England. It thrives in poorly drained, acidic soils where few other woody plants can compete. You'll often find it growing alongside red maple, black gum, and various sedges in these soggy environments.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge reddish and gradually turn green. Small, inconspicuous yellowish-green flowers appear in loose, drooping clusters.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed out with bright green compound leaves. Whitish berry clusters begin developing and are most noticeable during this season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant orange, red, and yellow before dropping, creating some of the most spectacular fall color in the swamp. Pale berries persist on bare stems.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show smooth gray bark and persistent whitish berry clusters that help with identification. The wetland habitat and drooping fruit clusters are key winter ID features.

funFact: Poison sumac is actually considered more potent than poison ivy, with some people developing severe reactions just from being near the plant when it's windy, as tiny particles of the urushiol oil can become airborne and cause skin irritation without any direct contact.
confusionNotes: The most dangerous confusion is with staghorn sumac and smooth sumac, which have similar compound leaves but grow in dry, upland areas and have red berry clusters that point upward like candles. Remember: 'Red berries overhead, you're fine ahead; white berries that droop, stay out of the group!' Also, harmless sumacs have toothed leaflet edges while poison sumac's leaflets have smooth edges.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sumac,' poison sumac is more closely related to poison ivy and poison oak than to the harmless sumacs people use for landscaping. All are in the cashew family, but they're in different genera. The name confusion has led to many misidentifications, so always check the habitat, berry color, and leaflet edges before making assumptions based on the name alone.
compareHints: Compared to eastern poison ivy, poison sumac is much larger (a tree/shrub vs. a vine or low shrub), has many more leaflets (7-13 vs. 3), and grows exclusively in wet areas rather than diverse habitats. While poison ivy has the famous 'leaves of three,' poison sumac has compound leaves resembling those of harmless sumacs, making habitat the key distinguishing factor from its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern poison ivy differs from poison sumac by having three leaflets instead of 7-13, and poison sumac grows only in wetlands while poison ivy avoids wet areas.
Western poison ivy differs from eastern poison ivy by growing primarily as a low shrub rather than a climbing vine, and typically having more rounded, less serrated leaflets.
